title: Minimum Number of Flips to Make the Binary String Alternating
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing mismatch counts per rotation versus a fixed-size sliding window over a doubled string, tracking two mismatch counts in parallel.

content.title: Minimum Number of Flips to Make the Binary String Alternating

blocks.text: Given a binary string s, in one operation you may remove the first character of s and append it to the end (a rotation). You may perform this operation any number of times. Return the minimum number of character flips (changing a 0 to 1 or vice versa) needed so that, after some number of rotations, the string becomes alternating (no two adjacent characters are the same).

blocks.caption: Double the string to simulate every rotation, then slide a fixed-size window comparing against both alternating patterns

blocks.text: Given a binary string s, allowing any number of rotations (moving characters from the front to the back), find the fewest flips needed to make some rotation of s alternating.

blocks.title: Analogy: Testing Every Cut of a Circular Rope Against Two Rulers
blocks.text: Like having a circular rope of binary beads and wanting to cut it at some point to lay it out straight so it alternates perfectly. Doubling the rope's pattern and sliding a ruler of the rope's original length across it simulates every possible cut point, and checking each cut against both possible alternating rulers ("starts with 0" and "starts with 1") finds the cheapest fix.

blocks.caption: Sliding a fixed-size window over the doubled string simulates cutting the rope at every possible rotation point

blocks.text: A single character is trivially alternating on its own (there are no adjacent pairs to compare), so the answer is always 0 regardless of the character's value.
Before literally rotating the string n times and re-checking each rotation from scratch, notice that doubling the string turns every rotation into a fixed-size window.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Rotating s by k positions is exactly the substring of (s + s) starting at index k and running for n characters, so doubling s and sliding a window of length n across it covers every possible rotation.

Observation 2: An alternating binary string of a given length is always one of exactly 2 possibilities: starting with '0' (0,1,0,1,...) or starting with '1' (1,0,1,0,...). Every candidate window must be compared against both.

Observation 3: For a fixed target pattern, the number of flips needed for a window is exactly its mismatch count against that pattern; this mismatch count can be maintained incrementally as the window slides, adding the entering position's mismatch status and removing the leaving position's.

Observation 4: Track two running mismatch counts (one per target pattern) simultaneously as the window slides across the doubled string, and record the overall minimum across both counts and every window position.

Recognizing that doubling the string converts "try every rotation" into a fixed-size sliding window, and that only 2 target patterns ever need checking, turns an apparently expensive rotation search into a single linear pass.

This is the fixed-size sliding window pattern, tracking two running mismatch counts in parallel (one per possible alternating target), updated incrementally as the window slides across the doubled string.
For every possible rotation starting point, slice out the window from the doubled string and count mismatches against both target patterns directly.

items: Double s to simulate every rotation as a substring.
For every possible starting index (representing one rotation), slice out the length-n window and count its mismatches against both alternating target patterns from scratch.

codes.python:
def min_flips(s):
    n = len(s)
    best = n
    doubled = s + s
    for start in range(n):                                                  # try every possible rotation as a starting point
        window = doubled[start:start + n]
        mismatch1 = sum(1 for i, c in enumerate(window) if c != ('0' if i % 2 == 0 else '1'))
        mismatch2 = sum(1 for i, c in enumerate(window) if c != ('1' if i % 2 == 0 else '0'))
        best = min(best, mismatch1, mismatch2)
    return best


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(min_flips("1110"))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The doubled string is built once upfront, letting every rotation be expressed as a simple substring slice.
Both mismatch counts are recomputed directly for every rotation, since this version does not yet share work between overlapping windows.
best tracks the minimum across every rotation and both target patterns simultaneously.

blocks.text: Every possible rotation is checked directly against both target patterns, so the correct minimum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since each of the n rotations recomputes its mismatch counts over a window of length n.
Space: O(n) for the doubled string.

Limitation: recomputing both mismatch counts from scratch for every rotation ignores that shifting the window by one position only changes a single entering and a single leaving character, which can be tracked incrementally instead.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force recomputes both mismatch counts from scratch for every rotation. Instead, maintain two running mismatch counts (against each of the two target patterns) as a single window slides across the doubled string. Adding the entering character updates both counts by checking it against both patterns' expected value at that position; once the window exceeds size n, removing the leaving character's contribution similarly updates both counts. Track the minimum of both counts across every valid window position.

Slide a window across the doubled string. At each position, update mismatch1 and mismatch2 by checking the entering character against both target patterns' expected value there. Once the window reaches size n, also remove the leaving character's contribution to both counts. Track the minimum of mismatch1 and mismatch2 across every fully-formed window.
Slide a fixed-size window of length n across the doubled string, maintaining two running mismatch counts in parallel.

blocks.title: Continuing the slide
blocks.text: The remaining window positions [2,5], [3,6], [4,7] each also settle at a minimum of 1 (the full trace confirms mismatch1 stays 3 and mismatch2 stays 1 throughout), so the overall answer is 1, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass over the doubled string (length 2n) with O(1) work per character.
Space: O(n) for the doubled string.

Doubling s guarantees that every possible rotation of s appears as some contiguous length-n window inside the doubled string, so scanning all such windows covers every rotation exactly once. Maintaining both mismatch counts incrementally (adding the entering character's mismatch status, removing the leaving character's once the window is full-sized) avoids ever recomputing a window's mismatch count from scratch.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["i < n (window still filling)","Mismatch counts accumulate, but no comparison to best happens yet"],["i >= n - 1 (window complete)","Compare both running mismatch counts against the current best"],["i >= n (window sliding, not just filling)","The leaving character's contribution is removed from both running counts"]]}

items: Both mismatch1 and mismatch2 are updated for every character, since each new character must be checked against both target patterns.
The leaving-character removal only triggers once i >= n, ensuring the window never shrinks below length n.
best is updated only once the window is fully formed (i >= n - 1), avoiding comparing an incomplete window.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Any rotation is allowed, minimize flips/changes to reach some target property" points toward doubling the string to simulate rotations as a fixed-size sliding window, then tracking mismatch counts against every fixed number of possible targets in parallel.

items: How would you also report which rotation and pattern achieves the minimum? Track the window's starting index and which pattern (1 or 2) achieved the minimum at the moment best is updated.

What if flips had different costs depending on position or character? The running mismatch counts would need to become running cost sums instead of simple counts, but the same incremental sliding window technique still applies.

How would this generalize to a k-ary alphabet instead of binary? There would be more than 2 possible "alternating" target patterns to track in parallel (though for k > 2, "alternating" typically needs a more careful definition), scaling the number of tracked running counts accordingly.

A fixed-size sliding window problem using the "double the array/string to simulate rotation" technique, combined with tracking multiple candidate targets (here, 2 alternating patterns) in parallel rather than just one running sum.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (fixed-size sliding window, dual mismatch tracking): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window over a doubled string, tracking mismatch counts against 2 candidate alternating patterns in parallel
Core Idea: Doubling s turns every rotation into a fixed-size window; only 2 possible alternating targets ever need checking
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Every rotation of s is exactly some length-n window of (s + s), and there are only 2 possible alternating target patterns to compare against
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Double the string, slide a fixed window, track mismatches against both "0101..." and "1010..."
